summary: This note is an excerpt from Josh Kaufman's The Personal MBA explaining the concepts of convergence and divergence in groups. Convergence is the tendency of group members to become more alike over time (the basis of company culture), while divergence is the tendency of groups to become less like other groups. The note argues that the people you spend time with shape your behavior, so you can use convergence deliberately to adopt desired habits, and must sometimes break away from unsupportive groups to grow.
one_line: Josh Kaufman explains how group members converge in behavior over time and how groups diverge from one another, and how to use this consciously.
key_facts: Convergence is the tendency of group members to become more alike over time.
Divergence is the tendency of group members to become less like other group members over time.
In business, convergence is sometimes called a company "culture."
Group norms work like gravity: violate them and others will exert influence to bring the rebel back in line.
The proverb cited in the note is: "The tallest blade of grass is the first to be cut."
Divergence explains why fashions among the socialite class in New York City change so quickly and dramatically.
When the latest fashions appear in Target so people can imitate the look, fashions change to compensate.
The late Jim Rohn, author of The Art of Exceptional Living, said: "You are the average of the five people you spend the most time with."
Convergence can be useful if you consciously choose to spend time with people you'd like to become more like over time.
Josh Kaufman's client at a major medical research institution leaves work at 5:00pm instead of 7:30pm and is viewed by coworkers as not pulling his weight.
People who want to quit smoking or drinking often find it difficult because a large portion of their social network engages in those behaviors.
Joining support groups like Alcoholics Anonymous is described as a very effective way to change specific behaviors.
Once you realize how powerful convergence and divergence are, you can use them to your advantage: if your social circle isn't supporting your goals, change your social circle.
Friedrich Nietzsche wrote: "If you try it, you will be lonely often, and sometimes frightened. But no price is too high to pay for the privilege of owning yourself."
This concept is from Chapter 8, "Working With Others", of The Personal MBA.
